title: Augustine of Hippo
summary: Aurelius Augustine (354–430) was a philosopher and theologian from North Africa, bishop of the city of Hippo. In the Confessions he told the story of his life, his attachments and his inner struggles with a frankness unheard of in antiquity, and in The City of God he interpreted history as a contest between two kinds of love. His thoughts on time, memory, will and love influenced all of Western philosophy — from Descartes to Heidegger and Arendt.
onEmotions: Augustine argued with the Stoics, who considered strong feelings diseases of the soul. For him all feelings are forms of love: love reaching for what it loves is desire; love possessing it is joy; love fleeing what is contrary to it is fear; love feeling what is contrary to it is sorrow. So what matters is not to suppress a feeling but to understand what we love and how; rightly ordered love — the "order of love" (ordo amoris) — he considered the essence of virtue. Augustine saw the highest aim of love in God, but his observations on the restless heart, memory, habit and time hold true for the non-believing reader as well.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is a restlessness that won't let you settle, and there is nothing shameful in it. The very first page of Augustine's Confessions is about restlessness: the human heart, he writes, knows no rest. For Augustine this is not a malfunction but a sign that a human being carries a longing greater than any single thing can satisfy; he himself saw the ultimate aim of that longing in God. But his thought can be useful to a reader outside faith too: anxiety often says not that something is wrong with you, but that you want something very much — security, meaning, something to lean on. Augustine didn't muffle his restless heart; all his life he questioned it: what exactly is it looking for? A desire that has been named is less frightening than a nameless anxiety.
anxiety.practice: Finish the sentence "My heart is restless because it is looking for…" — several times, with different endings. Just see what comes up.

quote.text: You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.
quote.author: Aurelius Augustine

fear.text: Fear is natural: it appears when something dear to us is under threat. Augustine gave it a strikingly precise definition. In The City of God he writes that all feelings are forms of love, and love fleeing what is contrary to it becomes fear. And in one of his early works he notes that fear essentially has a single cause: dread of losing what we love or of not obtaining what we hope for. From this angle, your fear is not weakness but the other side of attachment. It shows what matters to you. Augustine didn't demand that we stop being afraid; he asked what exactly we love and what we lean on. When you see love behind fear, it becomes easier to talk with it.
fear.practice: Finish the sentence: "I'm afraid because I love…" See what turns up in place of the ellipsis.

sadness.text: Sadness is a legitimate feeling, and Augustine argued with those who thought otherwise. The Stoics saw strong feelings as diseases of the soul from which the wise must free themselves. Augustine objected: in The City of God he writes that sorrow is love feeling what it does not want, and that everything depends not on the feeling itself but on what a person loves. He recalled that Christ, according to the Gospel, wept — for him this was proof that sadness does not demean a person. Complete unfeelingness he considered not a virtue but rather a hardening of the soul into stone. So your sadness is not a mistake to be corrected quickly. It says that somewhere nearby there is a love that is hurting right now.
sadness.practice: Ask yourself: what, or whom, or which part of my life is this sadness about? Write down one word — without explaining it.

grief.text: Grief is one of the deepest wounds, and Augustine knew it from within. In Book IV of the Confessions he tells of the death of a close friend from his youth. Everything around him became torment: his hometown, his father's house — everything reminded him of the one who was gone, and nothing could say to him any more, as it had when his friend had merely gone away, "Look, he'll be here soon." Augustine confesses that he became a great riddle to himself and that only tears were sweet to him. He isn't ashamed of this and doesn't hurry himself. Later, after his mother's death, he held back his tears for a long time — and when he finally allowed himself to weep, his heart found rest in them. His experience says: grief doesn't need to be hidden and doesn't need to be got through quickly. Tears are the language of love.
grief.practice: Allow yourself a few minutes today when you don't have to hold yourself together. If tears come, let them; if not, simply recall one living detail about the person who is gone.

loneliness.text: Loneliness can be sharp, even among people, and it doesn't make you any less. Augustine valued friendship enormously and described it tenderly. In Book IV of the Confessions he recalls what comforted him after his loss: talking and laughing with friends, reading together, being able to fool around together and be serious together, sometimes disagreeing without hostility, teaching one another and learning, missing those who were away and joyfully welcoming those who arrived. Out of such small things, he writes, souls are fused into one. Augustine has another thought too: he was convinced that God is closer to a person than they are to themselves — so loneliness is never complete. Even outside faith you can take something simple from this: closeness is built from small shared things, not only from big confessions.
loneliness.practice: Think of one small shared thing — a book, a joke, a walk — that you could share with someone this week. Just write it down.

anger.text: Anger is a strong feeling, and it often arises where something important has been touched. Augustine did not consider anger evil in itself: in The City of God he allows for anger that rises against injustice and wants to set it right. But he saw one danger in it. In the Rule he wrote for his community there is a Gospel image: take care that anger does not grow into hatred and make a beam out of a speck. A speck that is carried inside, nursed and not let go, becomes a beam over time. That's why Augustine advised ending quarrels as quickly as possible. This is not a demand to forgive immediately. It's more an invitation to notice: while anger is fresh, it is still a message about what matters to you, not a verdict on another person.
anger.practice: Ask your anger: what is it protecting? Write down one word — a boundary, a value or a person.

shame.text: Shame is agonizing: you want to vanish from other people's sight. Augustine wrote a whole book in which he openly tells of what he was ashamed of — the Confessions. In Book II he recalls how, as a teenager, he and his friends stripped someone's pear tree: they didn't need the pears and threw them to the pigs almost at once. The question tormented him for a long time: why? And he comes to an honest conclusion: alone he wouldn't have done it — he wanted to belong to the group. What matters is how he speaks of what is shameful: without self-abasement, wanting to understand. The Latin word confessio means for Augustine not only admission but also praise — gratitude that a person has seen the truth about themselves and has not been crushed by it. Shame spoken out, even on paper, loses some of its power.
shame.practice: Write one sentence about what you're ashamed of — the way an understanding chronicler would, without judgment. Then you can erase it.

guilt.text: Guilt says that you care how your actions affect others. Augustine took guilt seriously, but his Confessions show a particular way of living with it. He doesn't hide his mistakes — for example, he admits that he slipped away from his mother by deception, at night, sailing from Carthage to Rome and leaving her in tears on the shore. But he doesn't get stuck in self-flagellation either: he remembers in order to understand how it all happened and to see that life went on and what grew from it. From Augustine's point of view, one might say that guilt is needed not to chew over the past endlessly but to turn toward something better. Guilt, in this perspective, is not a lifelong brand but the beginning of change.
guilt.practice: Ask yourself: what would I do differently tomorrow if this guilt were already forgiven? Write down one small action.

envy.text: Everyone knows envy, and Augustine considered it one of the earliest human feelings. In Book I of the Confessions he describes an infant who can't yet speak but already turns pale and looks bitterly at his foster brother at the nurse's breast. Augustine looks at this without sentimentality, but without malice either: envy appears before we have a chance to choose it. His thinking about it is deep. In The City of God he writes that possession of a good is not diminished when someone else shares it with you. There are goods that can be shared without loss — knowledge, joy, friendship, truth. Envy is sharpest where it seems there won't be enough for everyone. Your envy points to what you want — and it's worth checking whether that good would really diminish if someone else had it too.
envy.practice: Name what you envy and ask yourself: what part of it wouldn't diminish if I had it too? Write that part down.

emptiness.text: Emptiness is a heavy sensation: as if there is nothing inside and nothing fills you. Augustine knew it. Recalling his youth, he writes that he became to himself "a land of want" — a hungry, barren country. His thought about emptiness is paradoxical and comforting. For Augustine, evil and emptiness are not an independent force but a lack of good, as shadow is a lack of light. Emptiness, from this angle, doesn't prove there is nothing in you — it shows the place where something is missing. And the fact that you feel this lack already means a longing for fullness is alive in you. Augustine considered this longing the deepest thing in a person and called its goal God. But even without that, you can start with a simple question: what exactly is missing right now?
emptiness.practice: If your emptiness were a cup, what is it waiting to be filled with? Write down the first thing that comes — even if it seems small.

confusion.text: Confusion — when thoughts won't come together and it's unclear where you are — is unpleasant, but there is a lot of honesty in it. Augustine searched for answers for more than ten years: he was a follower of the Manichaeans, then almost a skeptic who doubted whether anything could be known for certain, then a reader of the Neoplatonists. And he admitted confusion even before the simplest things. A famous passage in Book XI of the Confessions is about time: we all use the word with ease, but as soon as we try to explain what it is, the answer slips away. For Augustine this is no reason to fall silent but the beginning of inquiry. From his point of view, one might say that confusion is a sign that you have honestly come up against something bigger than ready-made answers. That's where real searching begins.
confusion.practice: Write down the question that confuses you most right now — as a question, without trying to answer it. A precisely named question already works as a landmark.

quote.text: What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to one who asks, I do not know.
quote.author: Aurelius Augustine

fatigue.text: Tiredness is a sign that you've been giving your strength for a long time, and it deserves respect. Augustine has a scene familiar to many worn-out people. In Milan, where he was a successful teacher of rhetoric, he was due to deliver a speech in praise of the emperor — full, as he admits, of lies. Walking down the street, worn down by worries, he saw a beggar who was joking and cheerful — and envied his lightness. Augustine realized that he was sinking under the load of ambition that he himself was dragging along and that only kept growing. His conclusion is not that one must drop everything. It is that part of our tiredness comes not from the work itself but from what we work for and how. It's worth asking: what in this load is mine, and what is excess baggage?
fatigue.practice: Divide a page into two columns: "tired from the work itself" and "tired from having to keep up appearances." Write one item in each.

boredom.text: Boredom often comes when you have to do the same thing again and again. Augustine wrote a short treatise about this — On the Catechising of the Uninstructed: a reply to a deacon he knew who found it dreary to explain the very basics to newcomers time after time. Augustine admits: yes, repeating what you've long known can be boring, and the boredom is passed on to the listener. His advice is unusual. He recalls how people showing a guest the beautiful places of their hometown begin to admire them anew themselves — because they are seeing through the eyes of someone seeing them for the first time. The main remedy for boredom, for Augustine, is not novelty but love and empathy, which make the familiar alive again. From this angle, boredom is not a verdict on the task but an invitation to change your angle of view.
boredom.practice: Take one boring task and imagine showing it to someone who is seeing it for the first time. What would they notice?

joy.text: Joy is a gift, and Augustine valued it highly. In Book X of the Confessions he writes that all people without exception want a happy life, and defines it as joy in the truth. He explains: many are willing to deceive, but no one wants to be deceived — so real joy for us is joy in what is genuine, not in appearances. Augustine also observed that joy that is shared grows: when many rejoice together, he writes, each one's joy is richer, because people warm and kindle one another. You don't need to do anything with your joy or test how solid it is. You can simply notice what in it is real and what it's about — and let it be.
joy.practice: Tell someone about one thing that made you glad today. Notice what happens to joy when it's shared.

love.text: Love is the center of all Augustine's thought. In the Confessions he says that his love is his weight: as heaviness draws a stone downward and fire rises upward, so love carries a person wherever they are moving. For him the question was never whether to love — everyone loves. The question is what and how. In The City of God he gives a brief definition of virtue: it is the "order of love" (in Latin ordo amoris) — when each good is loved according to its worth, no more and no less. Augustine saw the summit of this order in the love of God, but a non-believing reader can take much from it too. Your love is a force that steers your life. There's no need to be ashamed of it; it's only worth watching where it is taking you.
love.practice: Ask yourself: where is my love carrying me right now? Describe in one sentence how this "weight" feels.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a quiet and powerful feeling. Augustine's whole Confessions is essentially a book of gratitude: the Latin confessio means for him not only admission but also praise. He gives thanks even for what he can't remember — for his nurse's milk, for the people who cared for him when he was utterly helpless. Augustine often repeats, after the apostle Paul, a question that changes a great deal: "What do you have that you did not receive?" For him gratitude is not politeness but a way of seeing your life rightly: as woven from gifts, from other people's care and work. From this angle, gratitude doesn't make you smaller. It shows that you were never entirely alone in your own story.
gratitude.practice: Name three things or three people without whom you wouldn't be yourself today — starting with the earliest.

hope.text: Hope is what holds you when the present is hard. For Augustine hope was one of the three chief virtues, along with faith and love. But his thinking about time makes hope understandable to a non-believer too. The future, Augustine writes, does not yet exist; it exists only in our soul — as expectation. So hope is not a forecast but the way your soul is already turned toward what lies ahead. In The City of God he soberly admits: in this life we are happy in hope rather than in possession. This is not a reproach to the world but an honest observation: hoping is a normal form of human life, not naivety. Hope already changes how you live now — even if the outcome is still unknown.
hope.practice: Write down one thing you hope for, and one small action that is already turned toward it today.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a bittersweet feeling, and Augustine explored its workings with interest. In Book X of the Confessions he writes about memory as vast fields and palaces where the images of everything we have lived through are stored. He was amazed that you can recall a past joy without rejoicing, and a past sorrow without being sad. He even compares memory to "the stomach of the soul": what we lived through is kept there, but without its former taste. Nostalgia, from this angle, is a meeting with something that still lives in you but belongs to another time. For Augustine the past exists only in memory — in the present. So when you remember, you don't go back; you bring the past into today, and it becomes part of who you are now.
nostalgia.practice: Choose one warm memory and describe it by a single detail — a sound, a smell, a light. What from it would you like to bring into today?

craving.text: A craving is a strong wave of desire, and there's nothing shameful in it. Augustine wrote honestly about a similar struggle in Book X of the Confessions. He admits that every day he wrangles even with simple things like food: it's hard to tell where the necessary ends and appetite begins, because pleasure knows how to pass itself off as need. That honesty is valuable: a craving doesn't always show itself as a craving; it disguises itself as "I just need this." Augustine also held that every desire strives toward some good — it points to what we lack. So instead of fighting the wave head-on, you can question it: what are you really looking for — relief, warmth, calm, a breather? The wave rises, peaks and subsides.
craving.practice: When the craving rolls in, note the time and rate its strength from 1 to 10. After ten minutes, rate it again — and ask what it is looking for.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure, and Augustine described its workings with rare precision. In Book VIII of the Confessions he speaks of habit as a chain: from a distorted will comes lust, serving lust becomes habit, and habit that isn't resisted turns into necessity. The links of this chain, he writes, held him in harsh bondage. There were two wills in him — the old and the new — and they tore his soul apart: he wanted freedom and couldn't take hold of it. Importantly, Augustine did not see the way out in a single effort of will. The turn came to him through other people — through their stories, their example, their support. From this angle, the way out of the chain is not solitary heroism but something done together.
addiction.practice: Think of who in your life knows what it's like to try to break free. If you'd like, talk with such a person, or with a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: The morning after is a hard time: the body aches and yesterday keeps spinning in your head. Augustine wrote a lot about how a pleasure that promised joy leaves bitterness and restlessness behind — and about how easy it is to mistake a brief relief for a good. But the main thing in him is how to treat yourself on such mornings. The Confessions are an example of how to look at your own lapses honestly and yet without contempt for yourself. Augustine tells of his mistakes in order to understand, not to execute himself. He is sure that a person is not reducible to the worst thing that happened with them. From this angle, the morning after is not a reason for a verdict but a moment of clarity: what did I actually need yesterday? The answer to that question matters more than shame.
hangover.practice: Pour yourself some water, sit down and write, without judging: what did I actually need yesterday? One word is enough.

euphoria.text: Euphoria is a bright high, and there's no need to spoil it. Augustine knew moments of immense joy. In Book IX of the Confessions he describes how once, at Ostia, he and his mother stood at a window overlooking a garden and talked quietly — and at a certain moment it seemed to them that they were touching something eternal. It was, in his words, such happiness that they wished it could last forever. But he honestly notes something else as well: afterward they sighed and returned to the noise of ordinary speech. A high can't last forever, and that doesn't make it any less real. For Augustine such moments were a sign of what the soul longs for. You don't have to cling to euphoria with all your might; you can remember it — so as to return to it later.
euphoria.practice: Write down one detail of this high — what you see, hear, feel. Let it be kept.

crash.text: The drop after a high is a painful contrast, and many people know it. Augustine described something similar in Book VII of the Confessions. He tells how for a moment he seemed to rise toward clarity and beauty — and was soon thrown back by his own weight, which he called habit. He describes this fall without despair, as the natural course of things: a soul that has lived through a high remembers it but can't live at that altitude straight away. Importantly, the memory of the high remains: Augustine writes that he carried away with him a loving memory of what he had seen. From this angle, the drop doesn't cancel what was. It only shows that between the peaks lie valleys — and you can live in them too, remembering the heights.
crash.practice: Put a hand on your chest and tell yourself: "The high was real, and the drop is part of the path too." Note one thing from the high that has stayed with you.

panic.text: A panic attack is a frightening experience: a wave of terror sweeps over you, and the body seems to slip out of control. Augustine didn't describe panic in today's sense, but Book VIII of the Confessions contains a scene of a real inner storm. In a garden in Milan he was so seized by turmoil that he tore his hair, struck his forehead, couldn't find a place for himself — until he went off under a fig tree and let his tears flow. And the storm subsided. It is an honest testimony: even the strongest turmoil has a peak and a subsiding. Such a wave usually rises, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Right now you don't need to understand or decide anything — only help your body get through it.
panic.practice: Press your feet into the floor and take a few breaths with a long, slow exhale. Name out loud three objects you can see.

dread.text: A vague dread of the future is a heavy feeling, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. Augustine offers an unexpected support here — his thinking about time. In Book XI of the Confessions he shows that the future does not yet exist. It exists only in our soul, now — as expectation; he called this "the present of things future." So what feels like an inescapable disaster ahead is an image that lives in you at this moment. This doesn't make the feeling any less real, but it changes its scale: it is not a verdict but a state of the soul, which can change. Augustine wrote that the soul can not only scatter itself among fears about what does not yet exist, but also gather itself — return to what is here now.
dread.practice: Tell yourself: "Right now I am here, and this moment exists." Name three things that are in front of you right now.

fomo.text: The fear of missing out — the sense that life is happening somewhere else — is understandable in a world of endless possibilities. Augustine described something related and called it "curiosity" (curiositas) — a thirst to see and know everything indiscriminately, not for any use but for the sake of the impression itself. He admits that he too got distracted — by a lizard catching flies, by a dog chasing a hare across a field. For Augustine the trouble is not interest in the world but dispersal: a soul that reaches for everything spreads itself across many things and loses itself. His answer is recollection: not trying to be everywhere, but being wholly where you are. From this angle, what you've missed stops burning when the present is filled with your attention.
fomo.practice: Choose one thing you're doing right now and give it all your attention for five minutes. Notice what has changed.

sleepless.text: Insomnia is a hard state: the night drags on and thoughts won't let go. Augustine has a scene that may comfort you. After his mother's death he couldn't find peace; even the baths he had hoped would help did not. Then he did fall asleep — and on waking felt that the pain had eased a little. Lying alone in bed, he remembered the verses of his mentor Ambrose of Milan — a hymn about the night that restores rest to the tired body, relieves weary minds and loosens anxious sorrows. These lines calmed him. From this angle, the night is not an enemy but a time when the soul can gradually let go of the day. Even if sleep doesn't come, you can simply lie in the quiet: rest for the body is rest too.
sleepless.practice: If you can't sleep, slowly repeat to yourself one gentle line — from a poem or a song you love. Let it sound in the rhythm of your breathing.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds especially deeply because it comes from someone you trusted. Augustine was not naive about people. In Book XIX of The City of God he writes that even in one's own home there is no complete safety: hidden treachery can come to light where it was least expected — and the closer the person, the more bitter it is. He considered this one of the hardest sides of earthly life. From Augustine's point of view, one might say that betrayal shows not that loving and trusting were foolish, but that love inevitably makes us vulnerable. Your pain testifies that you trusted in earnest. This is not your mistake: trust is one of the finest human capacities, even when it has been abused.
betrayal.practice: Write: "I trusted because…" — and keep going. See what real things your trust was based on.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is the fear of losing someone you love, and it burns from within. Augustine describes it with astonishing honesty. In Book III of the Confessions he recalls a youthful love in Carthage: he wanted to be loved and achieved it, but along with it, he writes, he was lashed with the red-hot rods of jealousy, suspicions, fears, anger and quarrels. For Augustine jealousy is love that fears losing what it loves. In Book IV he adds an important observation: we suffer most when we cling to another mortal human being as though they were our only support and could never disappear. From this angle, jealousy is not a vice but a sign of how much this person means to you and how much you lean on them.
jealousy.practice: Ask yourself: what am I afraid of losing — the person themselves, or what they mean to me? Write down the answer.

resentment.text: Resentment is a pain that won't go away, and it is often justified. Augustine understood its power. In the Rule for his community he speaks of anger that, if not let go, grows into hatred and turns a speck into a beam. Resentment that is carried inside and relived again and again grows in exactly this way. That's why he advises ending quarrels as quickly as possible. But the key thing in Augustine is a thought from Book I of the Confessions: no enemy can harm us more than our own hatred of him. This doesn't mean you must forgive immediately or that the hurt means nothing. It means that resentment is your burden, and you have the right to set it down one day, when you are ready.
resentment.practice: Imagine your resentment as a stone in your hand. What is it like — heavy, sharp, cold? Ask yourself: what do I need in order to set it down one day?

heartbreak.text: A broken heart is one of the deepest human pains. Augustine went through it himself. In Book VI of the Confessions he tells how he had to part from the woman he had lived with for many years and with whom he had a son: she was sent away because an advantageous marriage was being arranged for him. He writes that his heart, which had grown into hers, was torn, wounded and bleeding, and that the wound took a long time to heal. Even the man who would later become a great philosopher couldn't get through that separation "rationally" — and didn't pretend he could. But Augustine also has a quiet observation: time does not pass idly — it flows through the soul and gradually changes it. Your pain is a testament to the depth of your love.
heartbreak.practice: Put your hand on your heart and say: "It hurts here because I loved." Stay with that for a minute, without hurrying.

impostor.text: The feeling that you're an impostor who is about to be exposed is agonizing — especially for those who have achieved a lot. Augustine knew a similar feeling. He was a brilliant teacher of rhetoric and received a prestigious post in Milan, but later called himself a "seller of words": he taught people to speak persuasively without caring much about truth. He felt uneasy about how much of his success was appearance. But there was truth in that unease too: he sensed a gap between what he showed and what he wanted to live by. From Augustine's point of view, one might say that feeling like an impostor doesn't prove you are unworthy of your place. Sometimes it is a voice looking for authenticity: not "who will expose me?" but "what do I want to do in earnest?"
impostor.practice: Write down one thing in your work that you do not for show but because you believe it matters. That is your authenticity.

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred is a very heavy feeling, and the inner critic can sound convincing. But Augustine would not agree with it. In Book VII of the Confessions he arrives at a thought that turned his life around: everything that exists — precisely because it exists — is good. Evil for him is not an independent entity but only a lack of good, like a hole in a fabric that doesn't cancel the fabric itself. This means that you yourself, as a living person, are at your root good. What you hate in yourself is, from this angle, wounds and lacks, not your essence. The Confessions were written by a man who saw his mistakes clearly and still told his story with hope. The voice of self-hatred does not tell the truth about you.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one thing in yourself that doesn't need to be earned: your breath, your curiosity, your capacity to feel. That is your foundation.

helplessness.text: Helplessness — when it seems nothing can be changed — is one of the hardest feelings. Augustine described it very precisely in Book VIII of the Confessions. He was amazed: the mind commands the hand — and the hand obeys; the mind commands itself — and meets resistance. He wanted to change, but the will could not compel itself. This was not laziness but an honest discovery: not everything can be overcome by a single effort of will. The way out, for Augustine, came through what he called grace — through help from outside, which reached him partly through other people and their stories. Even without faith you can take away this thought: helplessness is not a verdict. What doesn't work alone sometimes becomes possible with someone beside you.
helplessness.practice: Think of who could share with you even a small part of what now feels overwhelming. Just write down their name.

procrastination.text: Everyone knows procrastination, and Augustine described it perhaps better than anyone. In Book VIII of the Confessions he recalls how for years he put off the decisive step, telling himself: "Soon, right now, just wait a little." And that "little" dragged on without end. He compared himself to someone who wants to wake up but keeps sinking back into a sweet doze. And in his youth, he admits, he even prayed for change — with the proviso "but not yet." Augustine laughs at himself, but without malice: he sees that procrastination is a divided will that wants and doesn't want at the same time. From his point of view, the way out is not to scold yourself but to understand: which part of you doesn't want to — and what is it afraid of?
procrastination.practice: Ask yourself: what is the part of me that procrastinates afraid of? Write one sentence in its voice.

quote.text: Grant me chastity and continence, but not yet.
quote.author: Aurelius Augustine

uprooted.text: The sense of being cut off from your roots is understandable in a world where people move often. Augustine lived such a life: from little Thagaste in North Africa he moved to Carthage, then to Rome, then to Milan — and almost everywhere he was an outsider. In The City of God he gave this experience a deep interpretation: human beings, he writes, are pilgrims in this world (in Latin peregrini). For Augustine this is not a curse but an honest description of the human condition: no place on earth becomes a final home, and he himself hoped for a home of another kind. But the thought can comfort outside faith too: feeling uprooted is not your personal failure but the shared lot of people. And home can be sought not only in a place, but in those you love.
uprooted.practice: Name one person, one habit and one object that stay with you wherever you move. They are your home too.

overload.text: Overload — when there's too much of everything and you're being pulled apart — is not a personal weakness. Augustine described it with astonishing precision. In Book XI of the Confessions he writes that his life is a scattering, that he has been dispersed across times whose order he doesn't understand, and his thoughts are torn by a motley tumult. Time for Augustine is a "distension of the soul": we hold within us at once the memory of the past, attention to the present and the expectation of the future. When there's too much of all this, the soul is stretched to its limit. His answer is neither a sprint nor an escape, but recollection: reaching toward one thing rather than spreading yourself over many. From this angle, overload is a signal: the soul is asking not for a new effort but for a return to what matters most.
overload.practice: Out of all your tasks, choose one that truly matters today. Write it down, and set thoughts of everything else aside for five minutes.

unreality.text: The sense of unreality — when the world or you yourself seem not quite real — is frightening, and it's important to speak of it gently. Long before Descartes, Augustine reflected on doubting reality. The skeptics of his time claimed that nothing can be known for certain. Augustine answered them with a simple thought: even if I am mistaken, I exist, since someone who doesn't exist can't even be mistaken. And even while doubting, I know that I live, that I remember, that I want to understand. This is not an argument but a support: in the very experience of "it feels like nothing is real" there is someone who is experiencing it. From this angle, your existence is the most reliable thing you have, even when everything around seems shaky and far away.
unreality.practice: Tell yourself: "I am here, I feel, I breathe." Touch something with a distinct texture — wood, fabric — and describe three sensations.

quote.text: If I am deceived, I am.
quote.author: Aurelius Augustine
quote.source: The City of God, Book XI, ch. 26

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience. Augustine recalls how once, gazing into the depths, he trembled with love and dread at the same time. And in Book X of the Confessions he remarks with surprise: people set out on journeys to marvel at the heights of mountains, the waves of the sea, the broad flow of rivers, the expanse of the ocean, the courses of the stars — and pass themselves by. For Augustine awe is not only admiration for the world but also an invitation to look within: in human memory and the soul he found an abyss no smaller than the sky. From this angle, your awe at the world can also become amazement that you are able to feel this way at all. Let it last.
awe.practice: Stay for a minute with what stirred your awe, and then ask yourself: what in me is able to respond like this?

relief.text: Relief is the feeling of a weight leaving, and it's worth savoring. Augustine reflected on it in Book VIII of the Confessions. He asks: why is joy especially great after danger? Sailors who have survived a storm, a sick person who begins to recover — all of them rejoice more than if there had been no trouble at all. He also recalls the Gospel image: there is more rejoicing over the lost sheep that is found than over those that were never lost. Relief, for Augustine, is joy in which the memory of the fear you went through still echoes. That doesn't mean the trouble was necessary. But it does mean that relief is a full feeling, not just the absence of anxiety. Let it arrive completely.
relief.practice: Take a slow exhale and notice where in your body things have become lighter. Stay with that sensation for a minute.

calm.text: Calm is a precious state, and Augustine thought about it a great deal. In Book XIX of The City of God he gives a famous definition: the peace of all things is the tranquillity of order — a state in which everything is in its place. For him peace is not emptiness or inactivity but a harmony in which the soul's different strivings don't pull in different directions. All his life Augustine sought such peace, and his Confessions begin precisely with the thought of a restless heart looking for a place to rest. Your calm right now, from this angle, is a moment when everything inside has fallen into place. There's no need to ask whether it will last. You can simply be in it.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute, noticing that right now everything is in its place: breath, body, thoughts. Nothing needs to change.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a moment when something opens up and you want to act. Augustine described such a moment, one that changed his life. In a garden in Milan he heard a child's voice repeating in a sing-song: "Take up and read!" He opened a book lying nearby — and read lines that seemed addressed directly to him. For Augustine this was a sign from above. But he also has a more general thought: in the dialogue On the Teacher he argues that understanding cannot be taught by words from outside alone — a person recognizes truth from within, as if through an "inner teacher." From this angle, inspiration is the moment when something inside you recognizes the truth. It's worth listening to it and writing it down while it's fresh.
inspiration.practice: Write one sentence that expresses what inspired you. Don't edit it — just keep it.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude — joy at someone else's failure — is an awkward feeling that's hard to admit even to yourself. Augustine confessed to something similar. Recalling how as a teenager he stole pears with his friends, he writes that the pleasure wasn't in the pears themselves: what tickled his heart was laughing at how they had fooled the owners, who could never have imagined they were capable of it. Augustine doesn't pretend it was innocent, but he doesn't call himself a monster either. He asks: what was it that delighted me so? From his point of view, one might say that schadenfreude often feeds not on cruelty but on a thirst to feel your own strength or to belong with "your people." Having such a feeling is human. What matters is to notice which need it is really serving.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: what did this person's failure give me — a sense of justice, relief, superiority? Write down one word.

contempt.text: Contempt is a cold feeling, and sometimes it seems entirely justified. Augustine understood its roots. In The City of God he describes the "lust for domination" (libido dominandi) — the drive to stand above others, which, by his observation, itself takes a person captive: whoever wants to dominate ends up dominated by that very lust. From this angle, one might say that contempt is a relative of this drive: a way of feeling superior. But Augustine also has another principle, set down in one of his letters: love people and hate their vices. You can reject an action without despising the whole person. This is not a demand to soften at once. It's an invitation to look closer: what in this person stings you — and what is your contempt protecting?
contempt.practice: Write down what exactly in this person provokes contempt. Then ask: which of my values does it touch?

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong reaction of rejection, and it can concern people, situations or even yourself. Augustine had an important experience here. As a young man he was close to the Manichaeans for almost ten years — a teaching that regarded matter and the body as evil and the world as a battlefield of light and darkness. Later Augustine decisively rejected this idea: everything that exists, in his view, is at root good, and evil is only a distortion or lack of good. From this angle, disgust should not become a verdict on a whole person or a whole world. It may honestly point to something distorted and wrong — but behind it there remains what cannot be reduced to the disgusting. This matters especially if the disgust is turned on yourself.
disgust.practice: If the disgust is directed at yourself, name one thing in you that remains valuable, whatever is causing the feeling.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is understandable: when you've been hurt, you want the one who hurt you to feel the same. Augustine didn't deny the strength of this feeling. But reflecting on violence, he named what is truly bad in it: not so much the outward damage as the desire to harm, the cruelty of revenge, an unappeased and implacable spirit. For him revenge wounds first of all the one who nurses it. And in Book I of the Confessions he writes that no enemy is more dangerous than our own hatred of him. Wanting revenge is human; it says nothing about who you are. What matters is to notice what it is protecting: your pain, your dignity, your need for justice. These needs are real — and you can acknowledge them and look for a way to meet them without harming anyone.
revenge.practice: Write down what you'd like the person who hurt you to understand or feel. Then ask: what do I myself need for this pain to ease?

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at the people close to you is one of the most uncomfortable feelings, especially when you feel ashamed of it afterward. Augustine would explain it through his central idea: all feelings are forms of love. We get angriest where we love most, because there is more expectation there and more vulnerability. He describes his mother Monica warmly: her husband was hot-tempered, and she learned not to argue at the height of his anger but to wait until he had cooled down — and then calmly explain her side. This is not a call to put up with everything. It's an observation that anger and love can live side by side, and that the time for an important conversation is better chosen once the storm has passed. Anger at someone close doesn't cancel your love — it is often born of it.
anger_at_loved.practice: Finish the sentence: "I'm angry with him (her) because what matters to me is…" See what love stands behind this anger.

ambivalence.text: Mixed feelings toward someone close — loving them and not being able to stand them at the same time — can be very tangled. Augustine knew this kind of split from the inside. In Book VIII of the Confessions he writes that there were two wills in him, the old and the new, and their struggle tore his soul apart. At the same time he argues with those who believed that two different souls, a good one and an evil one, live in a person: no, says Augustine, it is one soul that doesn't want with its whole heart. And in Book IV he exclaims that man himself is a great deep. From this angle, your contradictions are not a sign that something is wrong with you or with your love. They are a sign of depth. Love and irritation can live in one heart, and one doesn't cancel the other.
ambivalence.practice: Divide a page into two columns: "what I love in him (her)" and "what I can't stand." Fill in both — not to reach a decision, but to see both truths.

guilty_relief.text: Relief you feel ashamed of is one of the most hidden feelings. It comes after a breakup, a departure, even after the death of someone close who had long been ill — and it seems like a betrayal. Augustine would say: don't rush to judge yourself. For him all feelings are forms of love, and love has many layers. Relief can be love for the other, whose suffering has ended, and love for yourself, which has finally been given a respite. Augustine considered right love of self normal and necessary: in the treatise On Christian Doctrine he notes that the commandment to love your neighbor as yourself already presupposes love of self. From this angle, relief and love don't contradict each other. They can live in one heart at the same time.
guilty_relief.practice: Tell yourself: "I feel relief — and I loved." Don't choose one. Let both be.

indifference.text: Indifference where something "should" move you is frightening: it seems something is wrong with you. Augustine tells of a similar paradox. As a schoolboy he wept over the death of Dido, the heroine of the Aeneid, which he read in class — and at the same time remained indifferent to his own life, which, as he later believed, was going the wrong way. Feelings, for Augustine, don't disappear; they are directed: love is always moving somewhere, but not always where it's "supposed" to. From this angle, one might say that indifference doesn't mean you're a cold person. Perhaps your capacity to respond is tired right now, occupied with something else, or protecting you from pain that is too strong. It is a state, not a verdict.
indifference.practice: Ask yourself: where in the past few days did I feel anything at all, however small? Note it without judging.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything and leave — a job, a city, a role you're sick of — is familiar to many, and there is nothing shameful in it. Augustine left places too. After his friend's death he moved from his native Thagaste to Carthage, because everything there reminded him of the loss. Later he secretly sailed from Carthage to Rome, tired of rowdy and insolent students. And he honestly asked himself: where can the heart flee from its own heart, where can I go to get away from myself? This is not a verdict on change — Augustine's moves really did change his life. It's an observation: some things we take with us. From this angle, it's worth asking: what exactly do I want to get away from — and which of it will come along with me?
escape.practice: Write two lists: "what I want to leave behind" and "what I want to find." The second list often says more than the first.

forbidden_attraction.text: An attraction that is "off-limits" — to someone unavailable, to the "wrong" person — can be confusing and unsettling. Augustine wrote a lot about desire, and his central idea is unexpected: every desire, at bottom, reaches toward some good. The disorder, for Augustine, is not in the desire itself but in its order — in how it relates to our other loves and commitments. Of his youth he writes: "I was not yet in love, but I loved to love" — he was drawn to the very possibility of love. From this angle, one might say that a forbidden attraction often points to what we are missing: liveliness, recognition, freedom, being seen. There's no need to judge yourself or to rush to conclusions. You can ask: what is my heart really reaching for?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Ask yourself: what does this person or this situation stand for, for me? Write down one word — not a name.

social_anxiety.text: Shyness and fear of being judged are hard: another person's gaze feels like a verdict. Augustine admitted that he, too, depended on others' opinions. In Book X of the Confessions he examines himself closely: he is pleased when praised and stung when criticized, and he finds it hard to tell how strongly this holds him — since praise and blame are always close at hand. He doesn't pretend to be invulnerable. But Augustine has a support as well: in Of True Religion he writes that there is no need to go outside — truth dwells in the "inner man." From this angle, one might say that others' judgment is just one view of you, and far from the most complete. You know more about yourself than can be seen from outside.
social_anxiety.practice: Before meeting people, tell yourself: "Their view is their view. I know more about myself." Notice what changes in your body.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty — not knowing what will happen — wears you out. Augustine knew this from his own experience. In Book VI of the Confessions he describes himself at thirty: he still didn't understand how to live and kept telling himself, "Tomorrow I'll find it; any moment now it will become clear." He wavered for years — and yet in the end he found his path. He also has a thought that can help. The future, for Augustine, does not yet exist — it exists only as expectation in our soul. So uncertainty is not an abyss ahead but the way your soul is now turned toward the unknown. From this angle, one might say that not everything has to be known in advance. For today, what can be seen today is often enough.
uncertainty.practice: Write down one thing you know for certain right now, and one thing you can do today. That is enough.

waiting.text: Waiting — for results, an answer, news — stretches time out agonizingly. Augustine explored exactly this sensation. In Book XI of the Confessions he writes that time is a "distension of the soul": we remember the past, see the present and expect the future all at once. Expectation, in his view, is the way the future already exists in us now. Hence his famous formula of the three kinds of present. This thought changes how we see things: waiting is not empty time that has dropped out of life, but also a way of living in the present. While you wait, there is memory and attention in you, not only expectation. His mother Monica waited many years for change in her son's life — and all that time she went on living, not merely waiting.
waiting.practice: While you wait, notice one thing from the "present of things present" — what you see or hear right now. Stay with it for a minute.

quote.text: The present of things past, memory; the present of things present, sight; the present of things future, expectation.
quote.author: Aurelius Augustine

regret.text: Regret over something done or left undone is heavy, especially when it seems too late. Augustine knew this feeling. Book X of the Confessions contains a famous exclamation in which he regrets the years lived far from what became most important to him. But what sounds in it is not only bitterness but also joy: late — and yet. For Augustine the past exists only in memory, in the present. It can't be changed, but it can be reread and understood anew. The Confessions are themselves such a rereading: Augustine tells of his mistakes to see how his life grew out of them. From this angle, regret is not the end of the story but the beginning of a new way of seeing it.
regret.practice: Write down one regret, and under it what you came to understand through this experience. Even one word is enough.

quote.text: Late have I loved you, beauty so old and so new: late have I loved you.
quote.author: Aurelius Augustine

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is a pain full of love. Augustine described it after his friend's death: following the poet Horace, he called his friend "half of his soul" and admitted that living without him was almost unbearable. He wasn't embarrassed by this longing. But Augustine also has another, remarkable thought. In his sermons on the First Letter of John he writes that desire enlarges the soul: as a wineskin is stretched so that it can hold more, so longing, by deferring its fulfillment, makes the heart more spacious. From this angle, your longing is not only pain but also something that makes you deeper. It shows how much this person means to you — and that this bond is alive in you.
longing.practice: Write this person a letter you don't need to send. Tell them what you remember and what you would like to say.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — grim news, wars, injustice — can be almost unbearable. Augustine wrote The City of God in a similar time: in 410 Rome, which had seemed eternal, was sacked, and many people were shaken and bewildered. Augustine didn't deny suffering and acknowledged that disasters fall on people indiscriminately. He offered a view of history as an intertwining of two "cities" created by two kinds of love: love of self extending to contempt of God, and love of God. For him the second city lives unnoticed within every age. Even outside faith you can take away this thought: alongside the history of destruction there always runs a quiet history of care. Your pain is a sign that you haven't turned away from the world.
world_pain.practice: Find in today one small example of care or kindness — someone else's or your own. Write it down.

rejection.text: Rejection — when you're not accepted, refused, pushed away — wounds deeply. Augustine knew well how much in a person depends on others' approval: in the Confessions he honestly admits how praise and blame affected him. But in one of his polemical writings, answering attacks, he wrote: let anyone think what they like about Augustine, so long as his conscience does not accuse him before God. For him the main measure was not how others see you but what is really in you. This doesn't mean rejection doesn't hurt. But it does mean it doesn't determine your worth. From this angle, rejection is something someone decided, not who you are.
rejection.practice: Finish the sentence: "I wasn't accepted into…, but that doesn't cancel the fact that I…" Complete it honestly and kindly.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned is one of the most ancient human fears. Augustine knew this story from both sides. He himself once secretly sailed away from his mother, leaving her weeping on the shore — and later described her grief with pain. And he knew how hard it is to lose: a friend, his mother, the woman he loved. For Augustine the fear of loss is the other side of love: we fear being deprived of what we love. He wrote that a soul is miserable when it is bound to what is mortal as though it could never disappear. But this is not a call to love less. It is an invitation to find supports that don't depend on one person's presence: in yourself, in other bonds, in what has already been between you and that nothing can undo.
abandonment.practice: Name three supports in your life that don't depend on one person. Even small ones.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is a pain full of longing and hope at the same time. Augustine understood how strongly one can want love. In Book III of the Confessions he writes of his youth: "I was not yet in love, but I loved to love" — he was drawn to the very possibility of love. He isn't ashamed of this thirst; he describes it honestly — and so makes it understandable to others. For Augustine love is the weight of the soul, the force that moves a person. From his point of view, one might say that love is never in vain, even when it finds no answer: it already changes the one who loves. Your unrequited love shows how great your capacity to love is. That capacity is neither a mistake nor a weakness. It will stay with you.
unrequited.practice: Write down what you love in this person. Then ask: which of these qualities lives in me too?

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most painful feelings: it strikes at your dignity. Augustine wrote about it in very grim circumstances. In Book I of The City of God, after the sack of Rome, he addressed people who had suffered violence and violation. He insisted: what is done to a person against their will does not stain their soul; the disgrace belongs to the one who humiliates, not to the one humiliated. For Augustine purity and dignity are a matter of the will and the soul, not of what was done to a person from outside. This thought is worth repeating slowly. From this angle, humiliation does not define who you are. Your dignity has remained with you, even if it's hard to feel right now.
humiliation.practice: Tell yourself: "What was done to me says something about them, not about me." Put your hand on your chest and stay with that.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is a heavy feeling that many people carry for years. As a young man Augustine was close to the Manichaeans — a teaching that considered the body and matter evil. Later he decisively abandoned this view. In Book XXII of The City of God he writes admiringly of the human body, of its proportion and harmony. He even remarks that the body has features that seem to exist not for use but only for beauty. For Augustine the body is neither a prison nor an enemy but a good creation; everything that exists is, for him, at root good. From this angle, your body is not a project to be fixed but something that already has value.
body_shame.practice: Name one thing your body did for you today: carried you, kept you warm, let you taste something. Note it with gratitude.

illness.text: Illness — when the body lets you down — is hard both physically and emotionally. Augustine knew this firsthand. In Book IX of the Confessions he tells how he developed chest pains and his voice grew so weak that teaching became almost impossible. And once a toothache was so severe that he couldn't speak — so he wrote on a wax tablet a request to his friends to pray for him. It's a touching scene: a brilliant orator deprived of his voice still found a way to ask for help. From this angle, one might say that illness is neither a defeat nor a reason for shame. It is a time when you can let others take care of you.
illness.practice: Think about what small help you could ask for today. Write to someone about it — even just a few words.

pride.text: Pride in what you've done is a healthy and well-earned feeling. To be honest, Augustine was wary of pride. "Pride" in the sense of superbia he considered the root of many troubles — when a person puts themselves at the center of everything and forgets where their strength comes from. But superbia is not the same as joy in something done well. Augustine constantly gave thanks for his gifts — his mind, abilities, friends, teachers — and didn't pretend they weren't there. From his point of view, one might say that healthy pride is joy in what you've done that sees it as part of something larger: you were supported, you learned, you worked. Such pride doesn't separate you from others but connects you with them. And you can enjoy it with a quiet mind.
pride.practice: Write down what you're proud of, and next to it who or what helped you do it. Take joy in both.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness, melancholy, is a special feeling that holds both sorrow and beauty. Augustine wondered about its nature. In Book III of the Confessions he marvels: why do people at the theater want to feel sad watching sorrowful stories, and even love that sadness? And in Book IV he asks: why is weeping sweet to those in bitterness? He gives no simple answer, but he notes that there is something in sadness that touches and draws us. From this angle, one might say that melancholy is not a malfunction but a particular way of feeling the world: it holds a sensitivity to what passes and a love for what has been. You don't have to drive it away. Let it stay for a while.
melancholy.practice: Put on music that matches your mood and simply listen to it, without changing anything.
